Bar and bat mitzvah. The terms mean son of commandment and daughter of commandment, and they refer to the coming-of-age ceremonies that mark a young person's transition to Jewish adulthood and religious responsibility.

A bar mitzvah traditionally occurs at age thirteen for boys, while a bat mitzvah takes place at age twelve for girls, though many modern traditions now align both at thirteen. At this point, the young person becomes religeable and responsible for observing the mitzvot—the commandments—of Jewish law.

The celebration begins with months of intensive preparation. The young person learns to chant a portion of the Torah, called the parshah, and sometimes also the Haftarah, which is a reading from the prophetic books. The first public aliyah—the call up to recite the blessings over the Torah reading—is the core ritual moment. This marks the celebrant's formal entry into adult religious life and their first public participation in the Torah service.

Traditionally, only boys were called to the Torah for these aliyot. Contemporary Jewish denominations have moved to affirm girls' equal participation in this ritual.

Following the synagogue service, a family celebration called a simchat bar or bat mitzvah takes place, featuring a festive meal that welcomes the young person into adulthood. The scale of this celebration varies considerably across communities. In Orthodox communities, the event may be relatively modest, while in Reform and Conservative traditions, elaborate parties and large social celebrations are much more common.

The young person often delivers a devar Torah, a speech about a passage from the Torah that demonstrates their understanding of Jewish texts and values. Many families also use the occasion to donate to charity or sponsor community projects in honor of the bar or bat mitzvah, reflecting the Jewish value of tzedakah, righteous giving.
